item.title: Canada could transition to full renewables by 2050, expert tells youth climate trial
item.description: It is “definitely” possible for Canada to transition to full renewable energy by 2050, an expert in environmental engineering and atmospheric science has told the country’s first youth-led climate ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: It is “definitely” possible for Canada to transition to full renewable energy by 2050, an expert in environmental engineering and atmospheric science has told the country’s first youth-led climate trial in Vancouver. Stanford University professor Mark Jacobson said the shift is technically and economically feasible — but there are social and political obstacles. Jacobson has developed sophisticated models and road maps to help cities, states and countries, including Canada, make the shift to renewable energy. Canada does not need to rely on fossil fuels, he testified Thursday, as he outlined how the country could meet its energy demands by tapping “humongous” resources and opportunities in wind, solar and geothermal, along with pre-existing hydroelectric capacity. Combine that with the electrification of energy and transportation and “Canada can do it,” Jacobson said of transitioning to renewables. “Whether it actually does it by 2050 is more of a social and political question.” Jacobson is a witness for 15 young plaintiffs in the trial underway in Federal Court in Vancouver, where they are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing Canada’s trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions. Electricity is significantly more efficient than combustion, Jacobson said. “By electrifying everything and providing that electricity from renewables, you use a huge amount less energy. In Canada, it’s like 60 per cent less energy,” he said. “There’s no more combustion, so you eliminate the air pollutants, you eliminate the global warming emissions.” Shifting to renewable energy would help avert deaths and cut the health costs associated with fossil fuels, Jacobson told the hearing. He said an estimated 6,900 people die each year from air pollution in Canada. The plaintiffs’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, told the court in her opening statement the case was not about the existence of climate change. Rather, it hinges on whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse,” she said. “The plaintiffs are asking this court to hold Canada legally accountable for its role in continuing and worsening the climate crisis that is causing harm.” This report by Brenna Owen, The Canadian Press, was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

item.title: Churchill River energy agreement with Quebec not open for renegotiation, says N.L.
item.description: Newfoundland and Labrador’s premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: ST. JOHN’S — Newfoundland and Labrador’s premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation. Tony Wakeham said Wednesday that the Newfoundland and Labrador government had already voted in favour of the non-binding agreement, which he unveiled in August alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney and former Quebec premier Christine Fréchette in St. John’s, N.L. “Let me be clear: we will not be renegotiating the deal, and will not entertain an attempt by anyone else wishing to renegotiate the deal,” he said. He made the remarks as reporters pressed him about whether final agreements would be signed before they were debated in the legislature. But there is also a new Parti Québécois government in Quebec that could ask for changes to the multibillion-dollar agreement. Wakeham said he has not heard any rumblings about Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wanting changes. “I think what I’m trying to do is just outline our position,” Wakeham told reporters in St. John’s. The proposal — which the government has called a definitive co-operation and implementation agreement — lays out plans for Hydro-Québec and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro to expand the hydroelectric capacity of the Churchill River, which cuts through traditional Innu territory. Carney has touted the proposal as “the largest clean energy investment in North American history” and his government has promised $10 billion in financing to help it along. In a Facebook post Wednesday, the grand chief of the Innu Nation in Labrador said Innu were not included in the energy negotiations despite the agreement proposing projects on Innu land. Jodie Ashini pointed to a social media post by Carney saying he met with Wakeham recently in Ottawa, and a public statement from Wakeham pledging to “keep engaging respectfully with the Innu Nation.” “How is meeting with the prime minister and discussing our lands and not having us at the table respectful?” she wrote. “There is no respect from the (Newfoundland and Labrador) government right now to the Innu.” “Come to Sheshatshiu and speak with us,” she added, referring to an Innu community in central Labrador where the Innu Nation has its main office. Ashini has accused Wakeham and his government of interfering with a cultural exhibit detailing Innu history in Labrador. She says the government believes Innu arrived about 300 years ago, after the Europeans. The position erases thousands of years of Innu history, she has said. On Wednesday, Wakeham said he would table all final energy agreements in the legislature and propose a special debate about them. He would not answer directly when reporters asked if those agreements would already be signed, but he was clear they would not be open for changes. The Parti Québécois did not immediately respond to a request for comment. St-Pierre Plamondon and his cabinet were sworn in last week, and Wakeham has not yet met with the new premier in person. “It’s coming,” Wakeham said. “He wants to come to Newfoundland and Labrador for a meeting. He indicated that to me in our last conversation, and I’m looking forward to that.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026. Sarah Smellie, The Canadian Press

item.title: Canada ‘well positioned’ to increase trade with Europe: TD report
item.description: As Canada looks to develop closer economic ties with the European Union (EU), a new report suggests there is billions of dollars’ worth of untapped demand for Canadian goods and services in Europe.
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: As Canada looks to develop closer economic ties with the European Union (EU), a new report suggests there is billions of dollars’ worth of untapped demand for Canadian goods and services in Europe. The report, published by TD Economics on Wednesday prior to the Canada-EU summit taking place in Montreal on Thursday and Friday, said current Canadian access to European markets is limited due to regulatory hurdles, geography and other factors. “These barriers notwithstanding, Canada is well positioned to increase its market share in the EU,” wrote report authors and TD economists Vikram Rai and Rishi Sondhi. They said this week’s summit is an opportunity to “build momentum and advance cooperation in priority sectors,” as Canada looks to diversify its trading partnerships amid an ongoing trade war with the U.S. “European demand increasingly overlaps with Canadian capabilities and the two sides’ strategic interest in diversifying economic ties,” the report said. “The upside for Canadian exports is meaningful. Product-level analysis suggests demand for nearly $60 billion in additional goods exports could exist, under certain conditions, including roughly $50 billion in energy.” The report listed the defence, energy, critical minerals, digital markets, and financial and other professional services sectors as those with the “largest long-term opportunities” in an expanded Canada-EU trade partnership. “The biggest gains will need to be unlocked through expanded infrastructure and deeper cooperation to expand investment, improve market access, and build new supply chains in critical areas,” it said. Trade currently limited The EU accounts for around five per cent of Canada’s total international goods exports, the report noted, roughly in line with Canadian exports to the U.K. and China. Last year, it amounted to $43 billion worth of merchandise, which was just one per cent of the EU’s total imports. “Canada’s main exports to the EU include crude oil, aircraft, aluminum, uranium, iron, canola, nickel and diamonds,” the report said. “Even with this hefty product mix, Canada typically runs a goods trade deficit with the EU. In 2025, it amounted to $50 billion, with Canada importing high-value manufactured products like pharmaceutical products, automobiles and medical instruments.” Trade, the report argues, is the “most obvious place” for Canada and the EU to deepen their economic partnership, and the report authors said there are two main ways to think about the opportunity. “The first is to look for products Canada already exports competitively but sells only in small amounts to Europe,” they said. “The second is to focus on strategic sectors – such as energy and critical minerals – where governments on both sides want to build new supply chains and deepen economic ties, even if trade is limited today.” Breaking down economic and trade barriers for goods and services is something both Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have advocated for as Canada and the EU discuss what a closer relationship will ultimately look like. This week’s summit may provide some answers, but there’s still a long way to go, the report authors say. “Much work will remain after the summit: securing capital and buyers, delivering timely approvals, expanding infrastructure, and easing certification and procurement barriers,” they said. “Ultimately, stronger demand, greater Canadian capacity and better market access – not a one-off diversion of trade – could make Europe a meaningfully larger export market.”

item.title: Gold getting set to rally: Brooke Thackray
item.description: After a strong rally in 2025, gold managed to continue its rally only briefly in 2026, and is now trading slightly above US$4,000.
item.content:encoded:
After a strong rally in 2025, gold managed to continue its rally only briefly in 2026, and topped on Jan. 28, 2026 at US$5417,21 (XAU gold spot price). It fell to $3,976.50 on July 16, 2026 for a decline of 27 per cent and is now trading slightly above $4,000. It has been a frustrating decline for investors that have long believed in the merits of gold. One of the stated reasons for the strong rally in gold is that governments were spending too much money and racking up huge deficits and debts driving up interest rates and that central banks were going to have to step in to save them by printing money. This central tenet for gold moving higher has not changed, and yet, gold has dropped significantly. So, why has gold been declining in value?

Although the long-term thesis that central banks will have to “print” money to save the economy is a long-term driver of the price of gold, there are a number of variables that can affect the price of gold in the short term. Two of the largest drivers are the direction of interest rates and the U.S. dollar. In the short-term, the price of gold can be greatly affected by rising interest rates. When interest rates are rising, the opportunity cost of holding gold increases. Since gold does not pay a dividend, it becomes less attractive. Another major factor in driving the price of gold is the U.S. dollar. Generally speaking, when the value of the U.S. dollar increases, the price of gold declines, as gold is priced in that currency. In addition, when the U.S. dollar is rising, it becomes a strain on countries outside of the U.S., in particular emerging market countries. It becomes more difficult for other countries to pay their U.S dollar debts and on the margin, some countries are forced to sell gold to protect their currencies. We saw this earlier in March of 2026 when Turkey had to sell or swap 60 tonnes of gold (over US$8 billion) to protect their currency in an environment of a rising U.S. dollar. Gold doesn’t always decline when interest rates or the U.S. dollar are rising, but the headwinds make it more difficult for gold. In particular gold tends to struggle when both interest rates and the U.S. dollar are rising together. There are times when gold can perform well in this environment, but it is difficult. USD & Interest Rates Affecting Price of Gold The above graph illustrates the relationship between the price of gold (gold line), the U.S. dollar (red line) and the yield on the U.S. Treasury Note 10 Year (blue line). The period from January 2025 to February 2026 (green box) is generally a period of a falling U.S. dollar and a declining yield on the U.S. Treasury Note 10 Year. There are some zigs and zags along the way, but the overall trend was lower for the U.S. dollar and interest rates. In this period, gold performed extremely well and rose to over $5,000. In comparison, the period from March 2026 to September (red box) is characterized by a rising U.S. dollar and a rising yield on the U.S. Treasury Note 10 Year. In this period, interest rates rose very fast. It is not only direction that matters, but also the rate of change. Rising interest rates did a lot of damage to the price of gold and it performed poorly in this environment. The good news is that the yield on the U.S. Treasury 10 Year Note has recently been trending lower. It is difficult to tell at this point if it is a sustainable trend, or just another zag. At the same time that interest rates have moved lower, the U.S. dollar has slowed its ascent. This combination of trends is a welcome environment for gold to perform well compared to the earlier 2026 environment. So far, gold has not managed to rally in the developing favourable environment. Sometimes there is a lag and investors should be patient. The market is becoming more favourable for gold, it has just not shown up in the price.
